sections.html:
• Name: Red Mangrove Crab
  • Scientific name: Pseudosesarma moeshi (previously Sesarma bidens and Dromia enythopus)
  • Minimum tank size: about 20 litres
  • Type: semi-terrestrial
  • Breeding: very difficult
  • Size (carapace): up to 4 cm; across the leg span 10–12 cm
  • Water type: freshwater/brackish water
  • Moisture: 70–90%
  • Substrate: any
  • Diet: mostly herbivore/omnivore
  • Temperament: semi-aggressive
  • Colour: red, black and orange

Red Mangrove crabs originate from Southeast Asia. They are widely distributed in Sumatra (type locality Deli), the Mergui Archipelago in the Andaman Sea, Sulawesi, Peninsular Malaysia, and the Gulf of Thailand.

These crabs are semi-terrestrial, living in or near lowland rivers, streams, or swamps, in close vicinity to the ocean and estuaries, with varying water salinities.

They are dominant components of the intertidal macrofauna of mangrove forests and other wetland ecosystems.

Red Mangrove crabs do not require a lot of space. A 20-litre tank can house 1 adult crab. One male and 1–2 females may be kept together in the same enclosure of 40 litres.

Males should not be kept together because of aggression and territorial fighting.

Stocking is one of the most important factors when keeping them as pets. Overcrowding is a major source of stress for crabs. In most cases, it leads to health problems, aggression and cannibalism.

Red Mangrove crabs can climb vertical surfaces and often use this ability to escape from the tank, so a tight-fitting lid is essential.

Keeping Red Mangrove crabs is not complicated because they have no special requirements. This species is also pretty hardy and can withstand varied ranges of water parameters. Nonetheless, to keep them comfortable and let them live a long life, their core needs still have to be addressed.

Land vs water ratio: Red Mangrove crabs are semi-terrestrial and prefer land over water. The land area should take at least 70–80% of the space in the tank or even more. At the same time, water is extremely important as well:

  • Red Mangrove crabs molt (shed their old exoskeleton) in water.
  • Water provides more hiding places and is generally a safer place.

These crabs cannot stay in water for a long time. They will drown.

Water bowl and water type: Red Mangrove crabs will be completely happy with a suitably sized bowl of water available to them 24/7.

  • The water only needs to be a few centimetres deep. It should be big enough to completely submerge the crab and nothing more. As long as water pools can completely cover their entire bodies, they will be fine.
  • It should also have some hiding places, because the crabs molt in the water.
  • Provide a variety of surfaces for them to get out of the water. Rocks or driftwood can also be placed in the water to create small islands that the crab can climb onto.

In the wild, they have access to freshwater and brackish water. Therefore it is recommended to provide:

  • a bowl of freshwater and
  • a bowl of brackish water.

Is it possible to give them only freshwater and skip brackish water? Yes. It may shorten their lifespan a bit, but overall they will be fine.

How to prepare brackish and freshwater: Never use plain aquarium salt or table salt to prepare saltwater. Use only special marine salt (such as Instant Ocean marine salt or similar). The target is 1.005 to 1.010 SG (up to 12 ppt).

Add about 30 ml of salt for each 4 litres of fresh water in a plastic bucket. Use a good hydrometer or refractometer to take accurate measurements.

  1. Stir the water properly.
  2. Let it sit for about 20–30 minutes.
  3. Stir again to ensure that the salt is entirely dissolved and evenly distributed.
  4. If the salinity is too high, add more freshwater; if it is too low, add more marine salt mix.

For freshwater, ideally use dechlorinated tap water, bottled spring water or distilled water. If using tap water, let it age for 24 hours before use, as the chlorine in it is toxic to them.
For a classic paludarium setup, these crabs thrive in water with a pH of at least 7.0–8.0, KH 0–10 and GH 4–16. Optimal temperature is 22–26 °C.

Red Mangrove crabs are classified as opportunistic omnivores (they have adapted to eating both animal and plant material, dead or alive). This means they will eat just about any food they find on the bottom of the tank.

Observations indicate that these crabs do not have a strong preference for high-protein food. For the best growth, feeds should contain protein at a level of about 20–30% of the diet.

In captivity, they will eat a wide variety of foods including:

  • Vegetables
  • Detritus
  • Leaf litter
  • Seeds
  • Frozen bloodworms
  • Detritus worms
  • Tubifex worms
  • Blackworms
  • Bloodworms
  • Earthworms
  • Freshly crushed snails
  • Dead fish or shrimp, etc.

Vegetables and leaves (for example almond leaves, dead beech leaves, oak leaves, etc.) should always be on the menu, as the crabs feed on these and require the detritus from the leaves.

  • Diet type: mostly herbivorous/omnivore
  • Food preference: leaves and vegetables
  • Feeding frequency: 3–4 times a week

How often should the food be changed? Crabs are slow eaters, so food can be left for 24 hours before removing it to prevent mould. It is best to feed them at night or in the evening because they are nocturnal animals that naturally eat when others sleep. This also recreates natural conditions.

How often to feed? Adult crabs should be fed 3–4 times a week. Do not let them starve or they can start cannibalising very fast.

Do they need calcium? Yes. Calcium is a crucial component of the exoskeleton and of overall health. Calcium can be found in:

  • kale
  • broccoli
  • spinach
  • cuttlebones
  • eggshells (dusted)
  • figs
  • nuts
  • wonder shells
  • oyster shells
  • seaweed
  • seeds
  • insects, etc.

It is highly recommended to keep a small piece of cuttlefish bone in the enclosure all the time.

Red Mangrove crabs have a very complex social behaviour. On the one hand this is a semi-aggressive and territorial species. On the other, they can often be found in groups.

These crabs have fascinating personalities. They are not very skittish and readily display aggressive postures towards anything around them.

Although they are primarily nocturnal, they remain relatively active even during the day. They are not fully aquatic; they are semi-terrestrial and prefer spending more time on land.

They are also amazing climbers. Given the opportunity, they will try to get out of any tank.

They are not diggers in the true sense, but they can push out some soil to make their own dens. In nature, they usually do that at the edge of water bodies.

They are pretty messy and destructive, and strong enough to redecorate a paludarium to their liking.

  • Social: No
  • Active: Yes
  • Peaceful: No (semi-aggressive)
  • Burrowers: No (generally)

Lifespan: there is currently no data on the maximum lifespan of Pseudosesarma moeshi in the wild. In captivity, they can live at least 2–3 years if appropriately cared for.

Red Mangrove crabs have a smooth carapace and a square-shaped body. Their eyes are located at the end of two movable eyestalks. The average size (shell width) of the adult is about 3–4 cm; across the leg span they can reach 10–12 cm.

  • Although these brightly coloured crustaceans have earned their common name from the red coloration of the carapace, they are not all red. There are other colour morphs and some individuals can even be purplish or dark violet.
  • Claws are red. The extreme tips of the fingers are yellow.
  • Dimorphism in claws is not present.
  • Their legs have almost the same coloration as the carapace.
Plants: it is possible to keep them with plants, but it is not absolutely safe. They may eat or uproot some plants in the tank.
